title: File Handling
description: Working with FILE*: opening, reading, writing, seeking, and proper error handling.
objectives: Open and close files with fopen/fclose
Read and write text and binary data
Handle file errors and EOF correctly

content.heading: Opening, Reading, and Writing
content.body: FILE *fp = fopen(path, mode); opens a file, returning a pointer to a FILE stream object, or NULL on failure (a missing file in read mode, insufficient permissions, and so on) — that return value must always be checked before use. Common modes: "r" (read text), "w" (write text, truncating/creating), "a" (append text), and their binary counterparts "rb"/"wb"/"ab". fprintf(fp, format, ...) and fscanf(fp, format, ...) are the file-based equivalents of printf/scanf. fgets(buffer, size, fp) reads one line (up to size - 1 characters, always leaving room for a null terminator) into buffer, and returns NULL at end-of-file or on error. fputs(str, fp) writes a string (without adding a newline automatically). fread(buffer, size, count, fp) and fwrite(buffer, size, count, fp) handle raw binary data, reading/writing count elements of size bytes each. Every fopen() must be paired with exactly one fclose(fp) once the file is no longer needed.

content.heading: Seeking and Error Handling
content.body:
fseek(fp, offset, origin) repositions the file position indicator (origin is SEEK_SET for absolute, from the start; SEEK_CUR for relative to the current position; SEEK_END for relative to the end), enabling random (non-sequential) access. ftell(fp) returns the current position as a long. rewind(fp) resets the position back to the beginning, equivalent to fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET) (and also clears the stream's error indicator).

EOF is a special value (typically -1) returned by several functions (like getc()) to signal end-of-file, distinguishing it from any valid character value; fgets() instead signals EOF by returning NULL. feof(fp) and ferror(fp) let you distinguish 'ran out of input normally' from 'a genuine read/write error occurred' after a failed read.

content.explanation: Both fopen() calls are checked for NULL before use. fgets() returning NULL is the standard loop-termination signal for reading a file line by line until EOF.

keyPoints: fopen() returns NULL on failure — always check before using the FILE* it returns
fgets() is the standard safe way to read a line, bounded by a buffer size, avoiding overflow
fseek/ftell/rewind enable random access within a file
Every successful fopen() needs exactly one matching fclose()
commonMistakes: Not checking fopen()'s return value for NULL before using it
Using gets() (removed from modern C standards) or an unbounded read instead of the bounded fgets()
Forgetting to fclose() an opened file, risking unflushed writes or an exhausted file-handle limit
